title: json.load()
summary: Parse JSON from a file object. The `s`-less twin of `json.loads`.
description: `load` reads from a file, `loads` from a string. Remembering which is which is easier if you read the `s` as 'string'.

parameters.name: object_hook
parameters.description: Called on every decoded object, for custom types.

returns: dict, list, str, int, float, bool or None.

raises.when: The content is not valid JSON. It subclasses ValueError.
The file is not valid text in its encoding.

examples.title: Read a config file
examples.code:
import io, json
fp = io.StringIO('{"host": "localhost"}')
print(json.load(fp))

examples.title: Handle a corrupt file rather than crashing

real_world_usage: Configuration files, cached API responses, and fixtures in tests.

common_mistakes.fix: Use json.loads for a string; load expects a file object.
A truncated or half-written file is normal in production. Catch it and decide what an empty or corrupt config means.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a round trip preserves types
common_mistakes.fix: Tuples become lists, dict keys become strings, and datetimes are not supported at all.
The platform default differs between machines. Always be explicit.

performance_notes: The C accelerator makes this fast, but it builds the whole structure in memory. For files larger than memory, use JSON Lines and parse per line, or a streaming parser.
security_notes: JSON parsing is safe in a way `pickle` and `eval` are not — it cannot execute code. But deeply nested input can exhaust the recursion limit, and huge input exhausts memory: bound the size before parsing untrusted data.
